summary.title: Feature Toggles (aka Feature Flags)
summary.one_liner: Feature toggles let you change system behavior without changing code, and learning the toggle categories (release, experiment, ops, permissioning) and how to implement them cleanly keeps their complexity under control.
keywords: how to manage feature flags in code
takeaways: Feature toggles fall into categories (release, experiment, ops, permissioning) that differ in longevity and dynamism, and each should be managed differently.
Release toggles let incomplete code ship to production behind a flag, enabling trunk-based development and separating release from deployment.
Toggle routers can be per-request, cohort-based, or config-driven, enabling canary releases, A/B tests, and internal-only testing in production.
Decouple toggle points (where a decision is made) from toggle decision logic, so changing a flag's scope does not require editing every call site.
Constrain the number of toggles and remove transient ones promptly, since toggles add complexity.
summary.summary: Pete Hodgson's martinFowler.com article introduces feature toggles through a story about a team rewriting a spline reticulation algorithm on trunk, then evolving from a simple if/else toggle to a dynamic toggle router with per-request, cohort, canary, and A/B testing use. It classifies toggles along two dimensions, longevity and dynamism, into release, experiment, ops, and permissioning toggles. The later sections cover implementation techniques, such as decoupling toggle points from decision logic and inverting control so modules do not depend on the flagging system, with JavaScript examples. The page text is cut off before the sections on toggle configuration and working with flagged systems.
